connector: It is 1827, on a plantation in Maryland. A girl named Harriet is not yet eight years old, and she already works from before the sun comes up until after dark. This is a true story, and this is its first chapter. Read for what one ordinary day tells you about her life, and watch where she looks when no one is watching her.

a.raw: the young slave girl watched birds fly north she dreamed of freedom
a.fixed: The young slave girl watched birds fly north. She dreamed of freedom.
a.why: Capital T to start; a period after ‘north’ ends the first sentence; capital S to start the second sentence about her dream.

b.raw: harriet rocked the fussy baby her arms began to ache
b.fixed: Harriet rocked the fussy baby. Her arms began to ache.
b.why: Capital H on the name Harriet; a period after ‘baby’ ends the first sentence; capital H to start the second sentence about her arms.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain which fact surprised you most, and why.
scholar.journal-q2: … and explain how the North Star at the end of the chapter connects to those stories.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say which single detail Sterling uses that proves it best.

fill1.h1: When you leave a room, you go ___ of it. Which part means out?
fill1.why: ex- means out: ex + it = to go out.

fill2.h1: Stretching your arm away from you sends it outward. Which part means out?
fill2.why: ex- means out: ex + tend = to stretch out.

fill3.h1: Putting something off means doing it later, after now. Which part means after?
fill3.why: post- means after: post + pone = to put off until later.

fill4.h1: A P.S. comes once the letter is already finished. Which part means after?
fill4.why: post- means after: post + script = written after.

eg: When the baby’s eyes closed, Harriet stopped rocking.
Harriet froze in the middle of a rock.
Harriet stopped rocking, slowly, so the baby would not wake.

notes.wgrd: The central idea is the one big thing a chapter is mostly about. Name the topic, collect three short facts, and put them together in one sentence.
vocab: A large farm where one crop is grown (in the South, often using slave labor).
A true book about someone’s life, written by another person.
To stretch out or reach further.
To put off until a later time.
notes.wordParts: ex- means “out of” or “former,” and post- means “after”: exit, extend, postpone, postscript.
notes.grammar: An adjective describes a noun. It tells what kind, how many, or which one, and it usually sits right before the noun: a cold spring, three geese.
notes.spelling: To split a long name, find the vowels, split between the consonants, and read each chunk. Names follow the same rules as any other word: Bal·ti·more.

transcripts.welcome: Welcome to Freedom Train. This is a true story about a real girl named Harriet, who grew up enslaved in Maryland and became Harriet Tubman. Today you’ll warm up, work with two word parts, read Chapter 1, and start a new kind of writing. Today’s question: what does one ordinary day tell us about Harriet’s life, and about what she dreams of?
transcripts.wgrd: This week’s reading move is finding the central idea. A biography gives you a lot of facts, and you don’t have to hold on to every one. Ask what the chapter keeps coming back to. Today, collect three small facts about Harriet’s day. Then squeeze them into one sentence about what Chapter 1 is mostly about.
transcripts.dol: The model sentence gives a place and a year, and every capital in it is there for a reason. The sentence to fix has two thoughts jammed together with nothing between them. Find where the first thought ends. Then make sure each thought starts the way a sentence should.
transcripts.guide1: Two small word parts this week, and both of them point somewhere. One points out. The other points later. People who write about history use them all the time, because history is full of going out and of what came after. Look closely at the front of each word before you decide what it means.
transcripts.morphology: Cover the front of each word and look at what’s left. Then put the front back on. Does the word mean going out, or coming after? Read the meaning on the right before you type. Once you can feel the difference between the two, you’ll start spotting them in words everywhere.
transcripts.vocabulary: Four words for a new kind of book. Two of them tell you what kind of place Harriet lives on, and what kind of book you’re holding. Two of them grow out of this week’s word parts. Read each sentence first, take the word apart, and make a real guess before you flip the card.
transcripts.grammar: This passage is full of describing words, and nobody is going to point at them for you. Read it once and hear only the bare nouns. Then read it again with everything in. What did the describing words add? Tap every one you find, and then try to say the rule in your own words.
transcripts.spelling: Long names can look scary, but they’re built from ordinary pieces. Before you tap anything, clap each long word out loud and count the beats. Names of places and history words follow the same rules as any other word. Find the ones with three beats or more.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Freedom Watch is about looking. Harriet is eight, and she can’t go anywhere she chooses. But nobody can stop her from noticing. Watch what she sees through the window, and what she thinks about while she looks. Sometimes freedom starts very small, as the right to wonder.
transcripts.read: Chapter 1 opens on a beautiful spring day outside, and a great deal of work inside. Keep track of what Harriet does, what she eats, and where her eyes go when no one is watching her. Near the end, something goes badly wrong. Notice who comes looking for her, and the question she asks him.
transcripts.copia: Here is one plain sentence from Chapter 1. It is only three words long. Your job is to say it three new ways. Give it a new beginning, swap in a stronger verb, and add where or how it happened. The sentence keeps its bones, but each version shows a slightly different moment in that room.
transcripts.guide3: Now you write. The chapter questions ask about Harriet’s hard day, about the stories she has heard about the North, and about the central idea. Use facts from the chapter, not guesses. Then Writer’s Workshop starts something new. This quarter you’ll write to report what you find, not only what you feel.
transcripts.chapter: The third question is the big one. Don’t just retell the chapter. Line up your facts about Harriet’s day, and ask what they add up to. What does Sterling want you to understand about this girl? Pick the one detail that proves it best, and put it in your answer.
transcripts.workshop: Last quarter you wrote opinions, and an opinion says, I think. This quarter you’ll do research writing, and research says, sources say. It’s a different job. An opinion only needs you. Research needs evidence you can point to. Today, write one of each about Harriet, and listen to how different they sound.

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Ask what each word is about: going out, or coming after?

why.t: In Chapter 2, Harriet’s mother, Old Rit, saves scraps of cloth from the Big House and sews them, late at night by the fire, into a patchwork quilt of green and brown and yellow. It is the family’s only treasure. ex- means out, and post- means after. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: The quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. ex- = out, post- = after.
